0.title: 3 John: Walking in Truth, Tested by Character
0.overview:
Third John is the most personal letter in the New Testament — a private note, fifteen verses, addressed by name to a specific individual. It never quotes the Old Testament, never rises to the theological heights of 1 John, never delivers a formal doctrinal argument. It is, in the best sense, a pastoral letter: warm, direct, full of the texture of real church life, and quietly devastating in its portrait of two men who could not be more different. Gaius receives it with joy; Diotrephes, the elder hopes, will hear of it with something closer to shame.

The author is again “the elder” — the same hand that wrote 2 John, by tradition the last of the apostles, the old man who has outlived everyone and carries in his body and his memory the full weight of what it means to have known Jesus. He writes to a man named Gaius, who is otherwise unknown to us outside this letter but who is clearly a person of some standing in his local congregation — hospitable, faithful, generous, walking in the truth. The elder loves him dearly and says so without embarrassment.

The letter’s world is the world of early Christian itinerant mission: travelling teachers and evangelists who moved between house churches, depending entirely on the hospitality of local believers for food, lodging, and a hearing. In 2 John the elder warned against giving that hospitality to false teachers. In 3 John he commends giving it generously to faithful missionaries — and confronts a church leader who has weaponised his position to control the flow of hospitality for his own self-aggrandisement. The two letters are mirror images: together they answer the question of how the church should handle the connection between hospitality, authority, and truth.

The character sketch of Diotrephes is one of the most memorable in the New Testament — a man who “loves to be first,” who refuses the elder’s authority, who drives out members who show hospitality to the missionaries. He is not a false teacher in the doctrinal sense. He is something perhaps more common and more dangerous: a man of genuine religious position who has confused the authority of his office with the authority of his person, and who uses the machinery of the church to serve his own pre-eminence. The elder names him publicly, without rancour, with devastating precision.

1.title: Truth, Hospitality, and the Test of Character
1.overview:
3 John is a personal letter to Gaius. The elder greets him (vv. 1–2), rejoices that he walks in the truth (vv. 3–4), urges him to keep supporting travelling missionaries (vv. 5–8), confronts the domineering Diotrephes and commends Demetrius (vv. 9–12), and hopes to visit soon (vv. 13–15).

Its theme is that truth is seen in character. Gaius shows the truth by opening his home to strangers who come in Christ’s name. Diotrephes denies it, not in his creed but in his conduct, by shutting people out so that he can be first. The church has known both kinds of men in every age.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The elder writes to one man he loves “in truth”, with a love grounded in the gospel they share. He prays that Gaius’s body and circumstances will do as well as his soul. That is a striking compliment: Gaius’s soul is healthy enough to be the measure for everything else.
verseByVerse.theology:
Love in Truth

The elder loves Gaius in truth and prays that all may go well with him as it goes well with his soul.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Gaius’s soul was healthy enough to be the measure of the prayer.

Now: Pray for the whole person, knowing the soul matters most.

verseByVerse.quote: The elder to the beloved Gaius, whom I love in truth. Beloved, I pray that all may go well with you and that you may be in good health, as it goes well with your soul.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The elder to the beloved Gaius, whom I love in truth. Beloved, I pray that all may go well with you and that you may be in good health, as it goes well with your soul.

Meaning first. 3 John is a personal letter from the elder to his friend Gaius, and the companion to 2 John: where 2 John warned against welcoming false teachers, 3 John commends welcoming true ones. The elder prays for Gaius’s health, as his soul is healthy (vv. 1–2), and has no greater joy than to hear that his children walk in the truth (vv. 3–4). He commends Gaius’s hospitality to travelling missionaries, strangers though they were, who went out for Christ’s name taking nothing from unbelievers; believers ought to support such people and so become fellow workers for the truth (vv. 5–8). In contrast, Diotrephes, who loves to be first, rejects the elder’s authority, slanders him, refuses to welcome the brothers and expels those who do (vv. 9–10). Gaius must imitate good, not evil; Demetrius is well spoken of by all (vv. 11–12). The elder hopes to come soon (vv. 13–15). Three men are named, and the letter quietly asks which of them you are becoming.

The setting. By word count in Greek, this is the shortest book of the Bible. Gaius was a common name, and several men called Gaius appear in the New Testament (Acts 19:29; 20:4; Romans 16:23; 1 Corinthians 1:14), but whether this one is any of them cannot be determined. He was a faithful member, perhaps a leader, of a church under the elder’s care, possibly converted through John (v. 4). The letter gives a glimpse of church life near the end of the first century: travelling missionaries, house churches, hospitality, and a power struggle with an ambitious local leader. The church has never been without its difficulties, and God has never been without his faithful people in the middle of them.

The elder to the beloved Gaius, whom I love in truth. “The elder” is the apostle John (2 John 1). “Beloved” (agapētō) is used four times in this short letter; the old apostle cannot stop calling his friend dear. “Love in truth” is sincere love grounded in the gospel. Love and truth again, as in 2 John.

Beloved, I pray that all may go well with you and that you may be in good health. “Go well” (euodousthai) means prosper, have a good journey, succeed; it is built on the word for a road, a good way. “Good health” (hygiainein) is be healthy, from which we get hygiene. It was a common wish in ancient letters; perhaps Gaius had been unwell. The apostle who wrote of eternal life and the true God also prays that his friend’s body will be well. God made bodies, and his servants care about them.

As it goes well with your soul. Gaius’s spiritual health was excellent. The phrase uses the same verb, euodoumai, that Paul uses when he prays that he might succeed in coming to Rome by God’s will (Romans 1:10). Gaius’s soul is on a good road, and John prays that the rest of his life would prosper equally. The soul sets the standard. A fine measure: how would your body look if it were as healthy as your soul?

Where a healthy soul comes from. No soul is born healthy. Jesus said that those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick, and that he came to call sinners (Mark 2:17). Gaius’s soul was going well because it had been healed, and the healing was costly: by his wounds you have been healed (1 Peter 2:24). The good road his soul was on had been opened by Christ. Bodies weaken and fortunes rise and fall, but a soul made whole by the Saviour is already on the road to the resurrection, where body and soul will be well together.

Where Christians differ: does this verse promise health and wealth to believers? The prosperity gospel uses this verse to teach that God wants every believer to be physically healthy and financially rich, and that faith secures it. Verdict: This is a conventional greeting and a personal prayer for a friend, not a promise to all believers. John prays for Gaius’s health; he does not guarantee it. Scripture shows godly believers who were sick (2 Timothy 4:20; Philippians 2:25–27) and poor (James 2:5), and teaches contentment (1 Timothy 6:6–10). It is right to pray for one another’s health and welfare, but God does not promise prosperity in this life. The prosperity teaching that uses this verse turns a greeting into a guarantee God never gave.

What it does not mean. It does not mean physical health is unimportant to God. He cares for the whole person. But spiritual health matters most.

Is it unspiritual to pray for health and ordinary needs? Not at all. Jesus taught us to ask for daily bread (Matthew 6:11), and Paul prayed for Epaphroditus’s recovery and rejoiced when God had mercy on him (Philippians 2:27). Praying for a friend’s health, job, journey or exams is an act of love, as John shows here. The danger is only in getting the order wrong: praying earnestly for the body while never praying for the soul, or treating God as a supplier of comforts rather than a Father to be known. Pray for both, and let the soul set the measure. Ask for health, and ask for holiness, and trust him with the answer.

In a sentence. From the elder, to my dear friend Gaius, whom I love in the truth. Dear friend, I pray that you may enjoy good health and that all may go well with you, even as your soul is getting along well.

On a Tuesday. Pray for a fellow believer’s health and welfare this week, as John did for Gaius. Then tell him you prayed, and ask how his soul is doing, not only his body.

For worship. God cares for the whole of us. The Lord who made our bodies healed the sick and fed the hungry, wept at a friend’s grave and rose with a real body, and he does not despise our flesh. Even now the risen Christ wears a human body at the Father’s right hand, the pledge that ours are not forgotten. He prays for his friends as John prayed for Gaius, and his prayer reaches further: not only that it may go well with us on the road, but that we may be with him where he is (John 17:24).
verseByVerse.note: By word count in Greek, the shortest book of the Bible. Gaius was a common name; this one is otherwise unknown.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Travelling believers have told the elder that Gaius is “walking in the truth”, and they know because they experienced his hospitality. Truth is not only believed; it is lived, even towards strangers. The elder says he has no greater joy than to hear that his children are walking in the truth.
verseByVerse.theology:
No Greater Joy

Travelling brothers testified to Gaius’s truth. The elder’s greatest joy is hearing that his children walk in the truth.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Gaius’s faithfulness was known by what others experienced of it.

Now: A life that walks in truth leaves traces others can see.

verseByVerse.quote: For I rejoiced greatly when the brothers came and testified to your truth, as indeed you are walking in the truth. I have no greater joy than to hear that my children are walking in the truth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For I rejoiced greatly when the brothers came and testified to your truth, as indeed you are walking in the truth. I have no greater joy than to hear that my children are walking in the truth.

For I rejoiced greatly when the brothers came and testified to your truth. “The brothers” are travelling missionaries who had stayed with Gaius and reported back, probably the same men he had received in verses 5–8. “Testified” (martyrountōn) means kept bearing witness. “Your truth” is Gaius’s faithfulness to the gospel. Not the truth in the abstract, but your truth: the truth had become visible in Gaius’s faithfulness in practice.

As indeed you are walking in the truth. Not merely believing the truth, but living it: belief and behaviour consistent with the gospel (2 John 4).

I have no greater joy than to hear that my children are walking in the truth. “Greater” (meizoteran) is a doubly comparative form, emphasising: no joy greater than this. “My children” (ta ema tekna) are spiritual children, those he led to Christ or pastored. The greatest joy of a Christian leader, or parent, is not success, wealth or recognition, but seeing those in their care living faithfully (1 Thessalonians 2:19–20; Philippians 4:1).

What an old man counts as his greatest joy. Consider what this man had seen. He had been called from his father’s boat by the Son of God. He had seen water become wine, the dead raised, the Lord transfigured. He had stood at the cross, run to the empty tomb, and eaten fish with the risen Christ on the beach. And he says: I have no greater joy than this, that my children walk in the truth. Not his experiences, but their faithfulness. That is the heart of a true shepherd.

The joy John learned from Jesus. John knew where this joy came from. On the night before the cross he had heard Jesus pray for his disciples: I have manifested your name to the people whom you gave me, and they have kept your word (John 17:6). The Lord spoke of keeping them and losing none (17:12), and he asked that they might have his joy fulfilled in themselves (17:13). The Shepherd’s gladness over sheep who keep the Father’s word became the gladness of the under-shepherd. When John says he has no greater joy, he is sharing in Christ’s own joy over his people.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the elder took credit for their faithfulness. Their walk was God’s work; his joy was in seeing it.

I have no spiritual children. Does this joy apply to me? Most believers have more spiritual children than they realise: the children in your Sunday school class, the younger believer you encouraged, the friend you brought to church, the colleague who first heard of Christ from you, your own sons and daughters. And if you have none yet, you may pray to have some, and look for one person to invest in. But this joy is also available through others: you can share the elder’s gladness whenever you hear that any believer is walking in the truth. It is a family joy, and it belongs to everyone who loves the family.

In a sentence. It gave me great joy when some believers came and testified about your faithfulness to the truth, telling how you continue to walk in it. I have no greater joy than to hear that my children are walking in the truth.

On a Tuesday. Whose faithfulness brings you joy? Tell them. Write to a former pastor, teacher or mentor and tell him you are still walking in the truth; it will be one of the best letters he receives this year. And pray for those you are responsible for to walk in the truth.

For worship. The joy of the elder is a small window onto the joy of God. The Father rejoices over his children who walk in the truth; heaven rejoices over one sinner who repents. The Good Shepherd laid down his life for his sheep and lays them on his shoulders rejoicing when he finds them. His greatest joy, for which he endured the cross, is a people walking in his truth, and he will have them, every one.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: This is the other side of 2 John 10–11. There John forbids hosting false teachers; here he commends hosting faithful missionaries. The same act, opening your home, can betray the gospel or advance it, depending on whom you welcome. Those who support gospel workers become “fellow workers for the truth.”
verseByVerse.theology:
Fellow Workers for the Truth

Welcoming faithful missionaries makes the host a fellow worker for the truth. Receiving them is the counterpart of refusing the deceivers in 2 John.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The missionaries took nothing from the Gentiles and relied on the churches.

Now: Those who support gospel workers share their work.

verseByVerse.quote: Beloved, it is a faithful thing you do in all your efforts for these brothers, strangers as they are, who testified to your love before the church. You will do well to send them on their journey in a manner worthy of God. For they have gone out for the sake of the name, accepting nothing from the Gentiles. Therefore we ought to support people like these, that we may be fellow workers for the truth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Beloved, it is a faithful thing you do in all your efforts for these brothers, strangers as they are, who testified to your love before the church. You will do well to send them on their journey in a manner worthy of God. For they have gone out for the sake of the name, accepting nothing from the Gentiles. Therefore we ought to support people like these, that we may be fellow workers for the truth.

Beloved, it is a faithful thing you do in all your efforts for these brothers. “Faithful thing” (piston poieis) means you act faithfully, you do a loyal work. Hospitality is an expression of faith. Gaius’s spare room, his table and his purse were acts of faithfulness to Christ.

Strangers as they are. Gaius did not know them personally, but welcomed them as fellow believers (Hebrews 13:2; Romans 12:13). The New Testament word for hospitality, philoxenia, means love of strangers: not entertaining friends but opening the door to people you do not know because they belong to Christ.

Who testified to your love before the church. They reported his love publicly to the elder’s church. Kindness done in a private house was spoken of in the elder’s church, and now in every church in the world.

You will do well to send them on their journey in a manner worthy of God. “Send them on” (propempsas) means help forward. It is a technical term for providing missionaries with food, money and supplies for the next stage of their journey (Titus 3:13; Romans 15:24; Acts 15:3). It was not merely bidding them farewell at the door but taking responsibility for their next stage. “Worthy of God” (axiōs tou theou) means generously, as God himself would treat them, for they are his servants. The standard is not what is comfortable or customary, but what befits someone representing the God who gave his Son for the world.

For they have gone out for the sake of the name. “The name” is Christ’s name (Acts 5:41; Philippians 2:9–10). John does not even need to say whose name; for the early church there was only one. It is the name God gave the Son when he had humbled himself to death on a cross, the name at which every knee will bow, and these men had left home to carry it to people who had never heard it. Jesus said that whoever receives those he sends receives him (Matthew 10:40). To house such men was to stand under the same banner, and Gaius’s guests were, in a real sense, the Lord’s own visit to his door.

Accepting nothing from the Gentiles. “Gentiles” (ethnikōn) means pagans, unbelievers. They did not take money from those they evangelised, so that no one could say they preached for profit (1 Thessalonians 2:9; 2 Corinthians 11:7–9). Travelling philosophers often begged for money; Christian missionaries refused, and so depended on Christians.

Therefore we ought to support people like these. “Ought” (opheilomen) means are obligated. “Support” (hypolambanein) means take up, receive hospitably, undergird. Supporting missionaries is a Christian duty.

That we may be fellow workers for the truth. “Fellow workers” (synergoi) are co-workers. Those who support missionaries share in their work and its fruit (Philippians 1:5; 4:14–17). The woman who gave a bed to a missionary in the first century has a share in every church he planted.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians should support every travelling teacher; 2 John warns against supporting false ones. It means faithful gospel workers deserve generous support.

How do I know which missionaries and ministries to support? Ask the questions this letter and 2 John raise together. Do they bring the teaching of Christ, faithful to the gospel and to Scripture? Have they gone out for the sake of the name, or for their own? Are they known and sent by a faithful church, with accountability, rather than self-appointed? Are they honest with money? Start with workers your own church knows and has sent, and get to know them personally: write, pray, ask for news. Give regularly rather than only when moved by an appeal. And give generously, in a manner worthy of God.

Must I host strangers in my home? What about safety? Hospitality is commanded of all believers (Romans 12:13; 1 Peter 4:9), but its form varies with circumstances. In John’s day it meant travelling Christians known through the churches, often carrying letters of commendation, as Demetrius probably did (v. 12). Wisdom is not unbelief: it is right to host people vouched for by your church, to think about the safety of children and vulnerable people in your home, and to offer hospitality in other ways, such as a meal, a lift or a gift, where a bed would be unwise. The heart of it is an open door and an open hand toward Christ’s servants.

In a sentence. Dear friend, you are faithful in what you are doing for the brothers and sisters, even though they are strangers to you. They have told the church about your love. Please send them on their way in a manner that honours God. It was for the sake of the Name that they went out, receiving no help from the pagans. We ought therefore to show hospitality to such people so that we may work together for the truth.

On a Tuesday. Support a missionary this month: give, write, host, or pray regularly. Become a fellow worker for the truth. Ask your church for the name of one worker it supports, and send him a message this week asking how you can pray.

For worship. The gospel has always travelled on hospitality, because the Lord of the gospel came as a guest. The Son of Man had nowhere to lay his head, and he let himself be fed and housed by women who followed him and by friends in Bethany. He who owns every house on earth was content to be welcomed, and now he opens his Father’s house, with its many rooms, to strangers like us (John 14:2). Every spare bed and shared meal given in his name is a small echo of the welcome he has prepared, and nothing done for the name is forgotten.
verseByVerse.note: Travelling missionaries relied on believers for food and lodging rather than taking money from pagans.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Diotrephes “likes to put himself first.” He ignores the elder’s letter, spreads malicious talk, refuses the missionaries, and puts out of the church those who want to welcome them. Everything flows from one root: the love of being first. Demetrius is the opposite, commended by everyone, by the truth itself and by the elder. Position does not reveal character; conduct does.
verseByVerse.theology:
Diotrephes and Demetrius

Diotrephes loves to be first; he rejects the elder, refuses the brothers and expels those who welcome them. Imitate good, not evil.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Demetrius had a good testimony from everyone and from the truth itself.

Now: The love of being first shows itself in whom it shuts out.

verseByVerse.quote: I have written something to the church, but Diotrephes, who likes to put himself first, does not acknowledge our authority. So if I come, I will bring up what he is doing, talking wicked nonsense against us. And not content with that, he refuses to welcome the brothers, and also stops those who want to and puts them out of the church.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I have written something to the church, but Diotrephes, who likes to put himself first, does not acknowledge our authority. So if I come, I will bring up what he is doing, talking wicked nonsense against us. And not content with that, he refuses to welcome the brothers, and also stops those who want to and puts them out of the church.

I have written something to the church. This is probably a letter now lost, though some think it is 2 John. Diotrephes ignored or suppressed it, and we cannot be sure of its contents.

But Diotrephes, who likes to put himself first. Diotrephes, whose name means nourished by Zeus, is otherwise unknown, apparently a leader in the church. “Likes to put himself first” (philoprōteuōn) is loving to be first. It is a rare word, occurring only here in the New Testament, and no earlier example of it is known; John may have coined it to name exactly what Diotrephes is. His problem was not false doctrine but pride: a craving for pre-eminence that turns every relationship into a contest for first place. It is the opposite of the humble elders Peter describes, who do not domineer over those in their charge (1 Peter 5:3).

Does not acknowledge our authority. “Acknowledge” (epidechetai) means receive, accept, welcome. Literally, he does not receive us. The same verb appears in verse 10 for his refusal to welcome the brothers. He refuses both the apostolic authority and the apostolic missionaries, and the two refusals are the same act at different levels.

So if I come, I will bring up what he is doing. “Bring up” (hypomnēsō) means call attention to, remind. John will deal with him publicly.

Talking wicked nonsense against us. “Talking nonsense” (phlyarōn) means prating, babbling, gossiping, making baseless accusations; it comes from a root meaning to bubble up, like froth on boiling water. “Wicked” (ponērois) means malicious. He slandered the apostle.

And not content with that, he refuses to welcome the brothers. He refused hospitality to the travelling missionaries, perhaps because they came from John.

And also stops those who want to and puts them out of the church. “Stops” (kōlyei) means hinders, forbids. “Puts them out” (ekballei) means throws out, expels. He excommunicated those who disobeyed him. It was an abuse of church discipline for personal power.

The disciple who once wanted the first seat. There is something moving in John being the one to write this. Long before, he and his brother James had asked Jesus for the seats on his right and left in glory, and the other ten were indignant (Mark 10:35–41). Jesus told them that whoever would be first must be slave of all, for the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many (Mark 10:44–45). Within weeks John watched him do it, and stood at the foot of the cross where the Lord took the last place. John had learned it, slowly, over sixty years. He knew Diotrephes from the inside, because he had once been him.

What it does not mean. It does not mean all church leadership is suspect. It is a warning against pride and abuse of authority, and a reminder that authority in the church is for service, under the apostolic word.

How should a church respond to a controlling leader like Diotrephes? John names the marks: he loves to be first, rejects accountability, slanders others, refuses fellowship to faithful believers and expels those who disagree. John does not ignore it; he says he will bring it into the open. A church facing such a leader should appeal to other elders, insist on accountability according to Scripture (1 Timothy 5:19–20), and protect those he wrongs. And putting faithful people out of the church is an abuse of discipline, not discipline: church discipline is for unrepentant sin, done by the church through a careful process (Matthew 18:15–17; 1 Corinthians 5), not for those who will not submit to one man’s control.

Is not naming Diotrephes in a letter just gossip? No. Gossip is talking about someone behind his back to harm him. John names a public wrong done by a public leader, in a letter to a responsible believer, and promises to confront him face to face. That is the opposite of gossip: it is accountability in the open. Some wrongs, especially the abuse of power, must be named, or the vulnerable go unprotected. But notice John’s restraint: he says what Diotrephes is doing, not what he imagines about his motives beyond what is plain, and he does not ask Gaius to start a campaign. He will deal with it himself, in person.

In a sentence. I wrote to the church, but Diotrephes, who loves to be first, will not welcome us. So when I come, I will draw attention to what he is doing, spreading malicious nonsense about us. Not satisfied with that, he even refuses to welcome other believers. He also stops those who want to do so and puts them out of the church.

On a Tuesday. Is there anywhere you love to be first? Ask God to make you a servant instead. Some signs to look for: needing to have the last word, resenting someone else being praised, wanting your idea chosen, finding it hard to take correction. Pick one of those this week and deliberately do the opposite.

For worship. The Lord of glory, who had every right to be first, took the lowest place. He knelt with a towel and washed the feet of men who were arguing about which of them was the greatest. He made himself nothing, and so God has highly exalted him and given him the name above every name. In his church, the way up is down, because that is the way he went, and every Diotrephes will be brought low and every servant lifted up.

verseByVerse.quote: Beloved, do not imitate evil but imitate good. Whoever does good is from God; whoever does evil has not seen God. Demetrius has received a good testimony from everyone, and from the truth itself. We also add our testimony, and you know that our testimony is true.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Beloved, do not imitate evil but imitate good. Whoever does good is from God; whoever does evil has not seen God. Demetrius has received a good testimony from everyone, and from the truth itself. We also add our testimony, and you know that our testimony is true.

Beloved, do not imitate evil but imitate good. “Imitate” (mimou) means copy, follow as an example; it gives us our word mimic. Do not follow Diotrephes’ example. This is the pastoral pivot of the letter: faced with Gaius, Diotrephes and Demetrius, the reader must choose whom to imitate. In the New Testament imitation is a serious moral category: be imitators of me, as I am of Christ (1 Corinthians 11:1). Character is formed by whom we model ourselves on.

Whoever does good is from God; whoever does evil has not seen God. These are the tests of 1 John in brief (1 John 3:6, 10). Conduct reveals one’s relationship with God. Diotrephes’ behaviour called his spiritual state into question. He held office in a church; John wonders whether he had ever seen God.

Seen in the face of Christ. What does John mean by seeing God, when no one has ever seen God (John 1:18)? He means knowing him as he has shown himself in his Son. Jesus said, whoever has seen me has seen the Father (John 14:9). To have seen God is to have looked at Christ by faith and been changed by what you saw, for believers, beholding the glory of the Lord, are being transformed into the same image (2 Corinthians 3:18). That is why doing good is the evidence: people come to resemble the one they gaze at. Diotrephes’ love of first place showed that he had never truly looked at the one who took the last.

Demetrius has received a good testimony from everyone. Demetrius probably carried this letter. “Good testimony” (memartyrētai) means has been well spoken of; it is perfect tense. John sets him against Diotrephes, and commends him so that Gaius will welcome him.

And from the truth itself. His life was so consistent with the gospel that the truth itself testified to him, the way a key that turns a lock testifies that it was cut for that lock.

We also add our testimony, and you know that our testimony is true. This is the apostle’s own endorsement (John 21:24). The testimony to Demetrius is threefold, like a legal witness: from everyone, from the truth itself, and from the elder. John stakes his full apostolic authority on the commendation of a man whose name we would never otherwise know.

What it does not mean. It does not mean salvation is earned by doing good. It means the life of those born of God shows itself in good deeds.

Does whoever does evil has not seen God mean that a Christian who sins is not saved? No. John means the pattern of a life, as in his first letter (1 John 3:6, 9), not single sins; he also says that anyone who claims to have no sin deceives himself (1 John 1:8). A believer who struggles with sin and runs to Christ is not the one John describes.

Whom should I imitate if my own church leaders disappoint me? First, imitate Christ, the only perfect example (1 Peter 2:21). Then look, as Gaius was told to look, for the Demetriuses: the believers, perhaps not in leadership at all, of whom everyone speaks well and whose lives match the truth. Read about faithful Christians of the past, whose lives have been tested to the end (Hebrews 13:7). Do not let a Diotrephes drive you from the church; one proud leader is not the whole body. And pray for your leaders, honour what is good in them, and speak to them humbly about what is not.

In a sentence. Dear friend, do not imitate what is evil but what is good. Anyone who does what is good is from God. Anyone who does what is evil has not seen God. Demetrius is well spoken of by everyone, and even by the truth itself. We also speak well of him, and you know that our testimony is true.

On a Tuesday. Choose a godly example to imitate this week, and be one for someone else. Ask yourself what you are copying without noticing: whose tone, whose habits, whose opinions? Choose deliberately, and remember that someone is probably copying you.

For worship. God has never left himself without witnesses. In every church troubled by a Diotrephes there is a Gaius and a Demetrius, faithful, generous, well spoken of by the truth itself. They are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works (Ephesians 2:10), small portraits by the Spirit of the one perfect life. And the truth that testified to Demetrius is not an idea but a person, the Son who will acknowledge each of his servants before the angels of God (Luke 12:8) and own them as his.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The ending closely matches 2 John: much to say, a hope to come soon, greetings from friends. The two letters were probably written about the same time. 2 John warns against false hospitality; 3 John commends faithful hospitality. John ends with “peace” and asks Gaius to greet the friends “each by name”.
verseByVerse.theology:
Face to Face, and Peace

The elder hopes to speak in person. He sends peace, and asks Gaius to greet the friends each by name.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: 2 and 3 John read as companion letters on hospitality.

Now: The church is a fellowship of friends known by name.

verseByVerse.quote: I had much to write to you, but I would rather not write with pen and ink. I hope to see you soon, and we will talk face to face. Peace be to you. The friends greet you. Greet the friends, each by name.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I had much to write to you, but I would rather not write with pen and ink. I hope to see you soon, and we will talk face to face. Peace be to you. The friends greet you. Greet the friends, each by name.

I had much to write to you, but I would rather not write with pen and ink. As in 2 John 12. “Pen” (kalamou) is a reed pen, cut from the reeds by a river and sharpened to a point.

I hope to see you soon, and we will talk face to face. Personal fellowship. Literally mouth to mouth again: the elder wants to sit with his friend.

Peace be to you. “Peace” (eirēnē) is the Hebrew shalom, the risen Christ’s greeting (John 20:19, 21, 26). In a church troubled by Diotrephes, a word of peace. It is singular, addressed to Gaius personally: the whole letter has been a conversation between the elder and one beloved man, and it closes as it began, like a father speaking to a faithful son at the end of a hard conversation.

The friends greet you. Greet the friends, each by name. “Friends” (philoi) is an unusual term for believers, echoing Jesus, who called his disciples friends (John 15:13–15). “Each by name” (kat’ onoma) means personally, individually, as the Good Shepherd knows his sheep by name (John 10:3). The elder who has loved Gaius, confronted Diotrephes and commended Demetrius by name closes by asking Gaius to do the same for everyone in his church: the pastoral calling in miniature.

What it does not mean. It does not mean only close friends are greeted. All believers are friends of Christ and of one another.

How can I have peace in a church torn by conflict? Peace begins with Christ, who is our peace (Ephesians 2:14), not with the conflict being resolved. Rest in him first. Then refuse to feed the conflict: do not gossip, do not take sides on personalities, and pray for everyone involved, including those who have wronged you. Do what is right where you have responsibility, as Gaius kept welcoming the brothers. Support faithful leaders who are dealing with the problem, as John promised to. Be a Demetrius, of whom good is spoken. And remember that the church belongs to Christ, who will put things right in his time.

In a sentence. I have much to write to you, but I do not want to do so with pen and ink. I hope to see you soon, and we will talk face to face. Peace to you. The friends here send their greetings. Greet the friends there by name.

On a Tuesday. Learn the names of three people in your church whose names you do not know, and use them next Sunday. Greet a fellow believer by name this week, and tell him you are glad he is your friend in Christ.

For worship. The elder put down his pen because some things cannot be said on papyrus, and the Lord has dealt with us in the same way. He has given us his word in writing, enough for life and godliness, but he has not promised us letters for ever. He has promised himself. For now we have him on the page, as Gaius for now had only the elder’s letter; one day we will see him face to face (1 Corinthians 13:12), and the Friend who laid down his life for us will finish in person every conversation the letters began.

1.text: <sup>1</sup>The elder to the beloved Gaius, whom I love in truth.<sup>2</sup>Beloved, I pray that all may go well with you and that you may be in good health, as it goes well with your soul.<sup>3</sup>For I rejoiced greatly when the brothers came and testified to your truth, as indeed you are walking in the truth.<sup>4</sup>I have no greater joy than to hear that my children are walking in the truth.<sup>5</sup>Beloved, it is a faithful thing you do in all your efforts for these brothers, strangers as they are,<sup>6</sup>who testified to your love before the church. You will do well to send them on their journey in a manner worthy of God.<sup>7</sup>For they have gone out for the sake of the name, accepting nothing from the Gentiles.<sup>8</sup>Therefore we ought to support people like these, that we may be fellow workers for the truth.<sup>9</sup>I have written something to the church, but Diotrephes, who likes to put himself first, does not acknowledge our authority.<sup>10</sup>So if I come, I will bring up what he is doing, talking wicked nonsense against us. And not content with that, he refuses to welcome the brothers, and also stops those who want to and puts them out of the church.<sup>11</sup>Beloved, do not imitate evil but imitate good. Whoever does good is from God; whoever does evil has not seen God.<sup>12</sup>Demetrius has received a good testimony from everyone, and from the truth itself. We also add our testimony, and you know that our testimony is true.<sup>13</sup>I had much to write to you, but I would rather not write with pen and ink.<sup>14</sup>I hope to see you soon, and we will talk face to face.<sup>15</sup>Peace be to you. The friends greet you. Greet the friends, each by name.
